question: Do sit-stand desk interventions reduce total sitting time or improve health outcomes in office workers?
contradictions: Direction of cardiometabolic evidence: Graves 2015 reports total cholesterol improving (p=0.049) with 'beneficial' FMD and diastolic BP changes [1]; MacEwen 2017 reports no change in any cardiometabolic marker despite a larger sitting reduction [5][8]. Not directly contradictory (different populations, durations, and marker panels), but the run cannot resolve which better represents desk-scale effects; neither is replicated.

Durability: Nelson-Wong 2021's title reports long-term maintenance of decreased workplace sitting [9], while Konradt 2022 found health/comfort effects faded by 24 months [2]. These concern different outcomes (sitting versus health/comfort), so they are tension rather than contradiction - but a reader cannot hold 'benefits persist' and 'benefits fade' simultaneously without noting the outcome mismatch.

scopeContract.decisionAtStake: Whether an office worker, employer, or workplace-wellness buyer should spend money and floor space on sit-stand desks (with or without a supporting programme): if desks cut sitting meaningfully but health outcomes stay flat, the purchase is a behaviour/environment change, not a health intervention, and should be justified and evaluated as such; if health outcomes improve too, it competes with clinical prevention spend.
scopeContract.keyQuestion: In adult office workers, do sit-stand desk interventions - desk alone or desk plus an organisational/behavioural programme - reduce total daily sitting time by a meaningful amount, and do any health outcomes improve in replicated trials?
assumptions: Population is sedentary desk-based adults, mostly in high-income countries; clinical and industrial-worker populations are out of scope.
Meaningful sitting reduction means roughly 30+ min/day, the lower band of the 30-100 min/day range workplace guidelines associate with benefit; smaller shifts are reported as modest, not dismissed.

Health outcomes that count are measured in-trial (blood pressure, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, weight, validated musculoskeletal pain scales); acute post-meal responses or single-arm biomarker wiggles do not count as health benefit.

Evidence base will be dominated by RCTs of 4 weeks to 12 months follow-up, most device- or questionnaire-measured, mostly from Australia, the UK, and the US; long-term adherence beyond 12 months is largely untested.
A health outcome counts as replicated only if at least two independent trials or a pooled meta-analysis point the same direction with acceptable precision.
whatWouldChangeTheAnswer: Device-measured RCTs pooling to under ~15 min/day sitting reduction would collapse the meaningful-reduction conclusion to no effect.

Two or more independent trials, or a meta-analysis, showing consistent improvement in the same health outcome (e.g. blood pressure or low-back pain) would flip the no-replicated-health-benefit expectation.
Evidence that sitting reductions fade or reverse by 3-6 months without continued support would change the conclusion from durable change to short-term displacement.
Systematic reviews grading the health-outcome evidence high-certainty would force upgrading any no-benefit statement to an honest unknown rather than a negative finding.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Sit-stand desks alone produce a modest sitting reduction (roughly 30-60 min/day) with no replicated improvement in health outcomes.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Pooled device-measured RCT effect under ~15 min/day, or desk-only trials showing replicated improvement in at least one health outcome.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Desks plus a structured programme (coaching, sit-stand goals, managerial support) cut sitting substantially more (roughly 60-100+ min/day), still without replicated health gains.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Programme trials showing sitting reductions no larger than desk-only, or programme trials with replicated health-outcome improvement.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Sit-stand interventions reduce sitting AND improve at least one health outcome in replicated fashion.
hypotheses.killCriterion: No two independent trials agree on the same outcome improving, or pooled effects on that outcome cross null.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Interventions largely fail to change total sitting at all once the novelty effect washes out.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Consistent reductions of 30+ min/day sustained to 6-12 months in device-measured trials.

perspectives.label: Meta-analyst
perspectives.lens: A primary-literature academic pooling RCTs, who distrusts self-report sitting measures, single-arm before-after designs, and cherry-picked outcome switching.
perspectives.query: sit-stand desk workstation intervention office workers randomized controlled trial sitting time minutes per day meta-analysis

perspectives.lens: An occupational-health practitioner who has run Take-a-Stand style programmes and believes the null-health reading underweights well-supported interventions; distrusts meta-analyses that lump weak desk-only deployments.

perspectives.label: Trial skeptic
perspectives.lens: A skeptical epidemiologist hunting the strongest counter-case: novelty-effect decay, publication bias, tiny underpowered trials, and outcome-shopping in industry-adjacent research.

perspectives.lens: A corporate real-estate or HR buyer deciding whether to purchase, who distrusts vendor marketing and academic measures nobody in an office actually feels; reads costs, complaints, and productivity.

summary: Sit-stand desks do reduce sitting time: the run's strongest evidence is a Sydney crossover pilot RCT (n=42, 4 weeks) showing a 73 min/workday device-measured reduction at work versus controls (p=0.004), with self-reported total daily sitting down about 80 min/workday (95% CI roughly -155 to -4), so the workplace reduction was not offset by more sitting elsewhere [0][7]; a separate study's title reports office workers maintained decreased workplace sitting long-term after its intervention, though the fetched record could not verify magnitude [9]. On health outcomes the answer is negative as far as the captured evidence goes: no outcome is replicated across two independent trials - the single positive signal is total cholesterol down 0.40 mmol/L (p=0.049) plus magnitude-based-inference benefits in flow-mediated dilation and diastolic blood pressure in one 8-week desk-only trial [1], while a 12-week trial in office workers with abdominal obesity found a ~100-160 min/day sitting reduction changed no marker of cardiometabolic risk [5][8], and an RCT with 24-month follow-up found health/comfort effects faded out [2]. On harms, the one trial reporting them found no relative worsening of musculoskeletal discomfort, with workstations self-reported as easy to use and without perceived productivity loss [4]. The evidence base is thin: the trialists themselves call for larger, more representative samples before population claims [3], the Cochrane Clinical Answer could be fetched only as citation-free metadata rather than its pooled estimate [6], and the majority of extracted claims were never verified.
answerFirst: Yes on sitting, no on health: in the best evidence this run captured, a device-measured crossover pilot (n=42, 4 weeks) found sit-stand workstations cut work sitting by 73 min/workday versus controls (p=0.004), total daily sitting fell about 80 min/day without displacement to evenings, and one study's title reports long-term maintenance - but no health outcome shows replicated improvement, and one trial in which a ~100-160 min/day reduction moved no cardiometabolic marker in 12 weeks argues desk-scale reductions may be too small or too short to matter clinically. Coverage warning: 12 of 22 extracted claims (55%) were never verified - cut by the verify budget - and no pooled estimate was captured, so this answer rests on a handful of small single trials plus title-level maintenance evidence.

hingeNumber.value: 73 min/workday device-measured sitting reduction versus controls (95% CI roughly -106 to -39, p=0.004)
hingeNumber.why: It is the only device-measured, control-condition sitting effect in the captured evidence; the sitting-reduction half of the answer rests on this one number plus the same trial's self-reported total (-80 min/workday). No pooled estimate was captured (the Cochrane Clinical Answer fetch returned metadata only), so a single small pilot is doing all the quantitative work.
hingeNumber.sensitivity: If the wider-literature pooled desk-only effect is near 40 min/day rather than 73, the conclusion 'desks meaningfully reduce sitting' survives; if pooled device-measured effects fall under ~30 min/day (or under the ~15 min/day noise floor), the meaningfulness claim collapses to no effect. A 10-20% move in this number does not flip the answer, but the answer does flip on which trial is trusted - one small pilot versus a future pooled estimate.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: Sit-stand desks alone produce a modest sitting reduction (roughly 30-60 min/day) with no replicated improvement in health outcomes.
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: Pooled device-measured RCT effect under ~15 min/day, or desk-only trials showing replicated improvement in at least one health outcome.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: Neither kill condition is met. The one device-measured effect is 73 min/workday ([0]) - above this hypothesis's modest band, not below 15 - and the only health-outcome improvement is explicitly unreplicated ([1]), while an independent desk-only trial moved no cardiometabolic marker ([5],[8]). Surviving, with the caveat that the observed magnitude comes from one small pilot and the no-replicated-improvement leg could reflect short trial durations rather than absence of benefit.
hypothesisVerdicts.preRegisteredBy: hypothesisNumber (subject, scope and added negation checked - NOT polarity, and not that the claim is identical)

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: Desks plus a structured programme (coaching, sit-stand goals, managerial support) cut sitting substantially more (roughly 60-100+ min/day), still without replicated health gains.
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: Programme trials showing sitting reductions no larger than desk-only, or programme trials with replicated health-outcome improvement.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim compares a programme-augmented arm against desk-only or quantifies a programme effect. The two perspectives designed to reach programme and practitioner evidence (programme champion, workplace buyer) returned no usable search results in this run, so the only long-term maintenance claim ([9]) is title-level and cannot size a programme effect. This is an honest gap, not a negative finding.
hypothesisVerdicts.preRegisteredBy: hypothesisNumber (subject, scope and added negation checked - NOT polarity, and not that the claim is identical)

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: Sit-stand interventions reduce sitting AND improve at least one health outcome in replicated fashion.
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: No two independent trials agree on the same outcome improving, or pooled effects on that outcome cross null.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: The trigger is met: exactly one trial reports a health-outcome improvement (total cholesterol, p=0.049, with magnitude-based-inference vascular benefits) ([1]), and an independent trial that produced a larger sitting reduction changed no cardiometabolic marker at all ([5],[8]). No outcome is confirmed by two independent trials, and no pooled health-outcome estimate was captured. Sitting reduction itself is supported, but the replicated-health-improvement condition fails.
hypothesisVerdicts.preRegisteredBy: hypothesisNumber (subject, scope and added negation checked - NOT polarity, and not that the claim is identical)

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: Interventions largely fail to change total sitting at all once the novelty effect washes out.
hypothesisVerdicts.killCriterion: Consistent reductions of 30+ min/day sustained to 6-12 months in device-measured trials.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: The kill criterion is not met: short-term reductions are real in the captured evidence ([0],[7]), and one study's title reports maintenance of decreased workplace sitting long-term ([9]) - but that record is title-only, does not state device measurement, and (per its publisher record, outside the confirmed claim) concerns a multicomponent intervention, so it cannot satisfy a device-measured 6-12 month criterion. The hypothesis is weakened, not killed, and durability remains the weakest link in the answer.
hypothesisVerdicts.preRegisteredBy: hypothesisNumber (subject, scope and added negation checked - NOT polarity, and not that the claim is identical)

strongestArgumentAgainst: The strongest honest case against this answer: both halves rest on a thin, selection-prone base. The sitting-reduction effect (73 min/day) comes from one 4-week crossover pilot in a single Australian health agency (86% female, n=42) with a rolling waitlist design, and the only long-term support is a paper title - while 55% of extracted claims were never verified, and verification was importance-ranked by the extractor, so any null or negative sitting trials among the 12 unaudited claims are systematically invisible; positive small pilots are exactly what survives such a funnel. On health, 'no replicated improvement' may be evidence of absence of adequate trials rather than absence of benefit: every captured health-outcome measurement comes from trials of 4-24 weeks (plus one 24-month comfort-outcome follow-up), far too short for cardiometabolic risk to move, and the one trial that did measure markers closely (n=25, 12 weeks, abdominal obesity) lacked power to detect the small changes a 3-4% shift in daily sitting could plausibly cause. A reviewer could honestly conclude: 'unproven, not disproven - and the sitting effect is probably smaller than the one pilot suggests.'
whatWouldChangeThisCall: A pooled device-measured estimate (Cochrane review or successor, fetched in full) showing average desk-only reductions under ~30 min/day would collapse the sitting conclusion from 'meaningful reduction' to 'marginal or none'.

Any second independent trial reporting improvement in the SAME health outcome (e.g., another trial with total cholesterol or blood pressure improving) would flip the no-replicated-health-benefit leg and revive hypothesis H3.
Device-measured follow-up at 6-12 months showing sustained 30+ min/day reductions would kill H4 outright and move durability from title-level to evidenced.
Auditing the 12 unverified claims: if any contains a larger RCT with null sitting effects, the 73 min/day anchor must be revised downward and the confidence downgraded.
A head-to-head trial of desk-only versus desk-plus-programme would test H2, which this run left entirely untested after its programme and buyer search perspectives returned nothing usable.
baseRate: Absent. The confirmed evidence contains no outside-view base rate - no figure for how often workplace interventions sustain behaviour change at 12+ months, and no pooled success rate for sit-stand deployments. The one adjacent signal, the authors' own statement that larger samples are needed before public-health impact can be determined [3], is a caution, not a base rate. Any projection of sustained real-world benefit from these trials is therefore running on inside-view optimism alone.

findings.claim: Sit-stand workstations reduce sitting at work by roughly 70-80 min/day in short-term trials: 73 min/workday device-measured versus controls (p=0.004) in a 4-week crossover pilot, and about 80 min/workday self-reported total daily sitting in the same trial, with no offset elsewhere in the day; one further study's title reports long-term maintenance of decreased workplace sitting.
findings.evidence: Claims [0] and [7]: ActivPAL-assessed work sitting -73 min/workday, printed CI sign-mangled ('106,-39', consistent with -106 to -39), p=0.004; total sitting -80 min/workday, CI consistent with -155 to -4. Claim [9]: title-only maintenance evidence (Ergonomics 2021; metadata-only fetch, magnitude and follow-up unverifiable; publisher records indicate a multicomponent intervention).
findings.citationCheck: supported - all three claims passed a 3-0 adversarial panel; the CI sign readings and the title-only scope are carried as hedges inside the claims themselves

findings.claim: No health outcome shows replicated improvement across independent trials. The single positive signal is one 8-week desk-only RCT reporting total cholesterol down 0.40 mmol/L (p=0.049) plus 'beneficial' flow-mediated dilation and diastolic blood pressure changes judged by magnitude-based inference - a candidate, not a replicated finding.
findings.evidence: Claim [1] (Graves 2015, n=47): the cholesterol endpoint is nominally significant; the vascular outcomes rest on magnitude-based inference, a method that does not yield ordinary p-value guarantees. Claims [5] and [8] (MacEwen 2017, n=25 with abdominal obesity, 12 weeks): despite a ~100-160 min/day sitting reduction, no marker of cardiometabolic risk changed in either group (all P > .05). The two trials measured overlapping markers and disagree in direction, with only one positive.
findings.citationCheck: supported - claims [1], [5], [8] each passed 3-0; the 'unreplicated' characterization is an inference across them, and the run captured no pooled health-outcome estimate that could confirm or refute it

findings.claim: Where health and comfort effects of sit-stand interventions were followed longest, they faded: an RCT with follow-up to 24 months found no significant intervention effect on musculoskeletal complaints and activation at 24 months.
findings.evidence: Claim [2] (Konradt 2022, seven waves plus 18-month-later follow-up, Bayesian structural equation modelling): 'no significant intervention effect after 24 months implying a fade-out'; earlier improvement velocity predicted later benefit. The abstract covers these outcomes, not sitting time.
findings.citationCheck: supported - 3-0 panel; scope explicitly limited to the non-sitting outcomes the abstract measures

findings.claim: Sit-stand workstations were well tolerated in the one trial reporting harms: no relative worsening of musculoskeletal discomfort or pain, self-reported ease of use, and no perceived productivity loss.
findings.evidence: Claim [4] (Graves 2015, 8 weeks, n=47): no harmful changes in musculoskeletal discomfort/pain relative to controls; acceptability and productivity are self-reports over 8 weeks only - longer-term standing-related discomfort is not covered by any captured source.
findings.citationCheck: supported - 3-0 panel; the verifier noted the productivity half rests on same-page Results text outside the quoted slice, both verbatim

findings.claim: The captured evidence base cannot support population-level claims: trialists themselves call for larger, more representative samples, and the run never captured a pooled estimate - the Cochrane Clinical Answer addressing the core question was fetchable only as citation-free metadata.
findings.evidence: Claims [3] and [6]: 'Larger scale studies on more representative samples are needed to determine the public health impact'; the Cochrane Clinical Answer record shows Cited by: 0 in fetched Crossref metadata and no abstract, so its underlying pooled estimate never entered this run's evidence.
findings.citationCheck: supported - the underlying claims passed 3-0; the leap from them to 'cannot support population-level claims' is the synthesist's reading, flagged as inference

caveats: Unanswered sub-questions: no pooled desk-only sitting effect was captured (sub-question 1 answered from single trials only); the desk-plus-programme effect (sub-question 2) is entirely untested - the programme-champion and workplace-buyer search perspectives returned no usable results; no physiology/mechanism source (sub-question 6) and no quantified cost or harm magnitude beyond self-reported acceptability (sub-question 7) were captured; the Cochrane certainty question (sub-question 5) is answered only by a metadata shell. Unverified claims: 12 of 22 extracted claims (55%) were never audited - cut by the verify budget, ranked by importance first - so claims an extractor rated tangential are invisible here even if they would have overturned the answer; this is a structural blind spot, not a clean bill. Weak sources: the maintenance evidence is title-only; two anchor trials have n=42 and n=47 with 4-8 week horizons; all sitting-effect numbers come from essentially one pilot trial. Dropped claims: none were dropped as unsupported at synthesis, but 12 unaudited claims were excluded from consideration wholesale. Time-sensitivity: the most recent trial evidence is 2022; pooled estimates published since would supersede the single-trial anchor immediately.
openQuestions: What is the pooled device-measured desk-only effect on workplace sitting with confidence intervals - the Cochrane review's own numbers, which this run could not fetch?
Does adding a structured programme to the desk increase the sitting reduction over desk-only, and by how much (head-to-head or adjusted indirect comparison)?
Do sitting reductions persist at 6-12 months when measured by posture-sensing devices rather than titles and self-report?
At what duration and magnitude of sitting reduction do cardiometabolic markers actually move, if any - is the 12-week null a power failure or a real absence?

evidenceBase.verdict: 6 citable sources, at or above the floor of 5.
evidenceBase.note: This run was NOT aborted for being thin, by design. A thin run is evidence about the retrieval path and has twice exposed a real bug; discarding it would hide exactly the signal worth having.

honestLimits.falseKillRateUnmeasured: This report kills claims. How often it kills a TRUE one has never been measured — here or anywhere in the published literature. Read `refuted` before concluding something is unsupported.
honestLimits.reliabilityNotValidity: `calibration` measures whether the panel repeats itself, not whether it is right. An LLM panel has been recorded agreeing with itself at alpha 0.77 while being systematically wrong. A high kappa never licenses 'the panel is correct'.
honestLimits.confirmedMeans: `confirmed` means 'survived a filter of unknown accuracy', not 'true'.
honestLimits.killRateMeans: The kill rate reports how much was removed, never whether removal was correct.
honestLimits.quotesAreLocatedInCode: Every claim's verbatim quote is searched for in the exact page text the extractor was shown, in code, before the panel votes - see `quoteAudit` and `stats.quoteLocation`. A quote the engine could not fully locate was assembled from more than one place or had wording added, and is a defect in the EVIDENCE regardless of whether the claim is true. `unverifiable` means the page was empty or the quote too short to judge, and is never evidence of fabrication. Measured over 30 real quotes on 2026-09-08: 93% located.
honestLimits.partialCitationsAreKept: A `partial` citation verdict means the page points this way but the statement adds scope, certainty or specificity the page does not carry. A partial panel SURVIVOR is restated to what the page carries and re-audited: a supported restatement replaces it (the original is kept in `restatedFrom`), and one that still fails is demoted like `unsupported`. A partial is KEPT only when no re-audited restatement came back (`restate.verdict` no-restatement or no-reaudit). Measured with injected defects: an inflated number, an invented attribution and an inflated scope all came back `partial`. Read `citationPartials` before quoting a number or an attribution from this report.
honestLimits.framingProvenance: scopeContract.provenance says, per field, whether the asker SUPPLIED it or the model DRAFTED it. A drafted assumption and a supplied one look identical in the JSON and mean opposite things: a supplied field is a decision to respect, a drafted one is a premise the run should have tested.
honestLimits.irrelevantSearchResults: stats.pickStarvation counts how often the source picker was handed search hits and chose NONE of them. A high rate means search returned results that were not about the question - a poisoned or rate-limited upstream engine - and NOT that the web is silent. searchHealth counts results, not relevance, so it reads as healthy in exactly this case.
honestLimits.archivedCopies: A source whose `via` is `wayback` was read from the Internet Archive, not live: the publisher blocked the fetch. `snapshotDate` says when the copy was captured, and it matters - the provenance lens judges recency, and an archived page is as old as its snapshot, not as old as today. The archive is used ONLY after a live read failed or returned an abstract-only stub.
honestLimits.abstractOnlySources: stats.fetchVia counts how each source was READ. `crossref-fallback` means the publisher blocked the fetch and only the abstract was available, and those sources carry `abstractOnly: true`. A claim verified against an abstract has been checked against a summary of the paper, not the paper.
honestLimits.searchCoverage: `searchDegraded` (top level) is true when the general web was tried and answered under a fifth of its attempts: the report then rests mostly on a scholarly slice (Wikipedia/Crossref), and its coverage gaps are a search artefact rather than evidence that nothing exists. stats.generalWebOkRate is that rate, and stats.searchHealth has the per-backend counts behind it.
honestLimits.citationAuditOff: This depth ran NO blind citation audit: no claim here was re-checked against its cited page, and the report must not read as vetted. Use standard depth or above when the checking matters.
honestLimits.singleRater: Mode A (stdio): one driving window played every role - extractor, every verification lens, the citation auditor, synthesis and critic - in one conversation. Lens independence and audit blindness are NOT guaranteed here; what did run in code was the schema shaping, the kill tally and the citation arithmetic.
honestLimits.evidenceChecked: 10 of 22 extracted claims were verified (12 unchecked: ranked out of the panel budget by importance then tier, or excluded as non-citable sources). Unchecked is not refuted - see evidenceBase before reading silence as absence.

processCritique.markedInSummaryMeans: how many flagged sentences were located verbatim and marked [UNTRACEABLE: ...] in summaryAnnotated, which is the ORIGINAL summary - under DR_UNTRACEABLE=strike the `summary` field has the same sentences removed. A flag the critic paraphrased cannot be located, so it appears only in untraceableStatements - read those too.
processCritique.untraceableCountMeans: distinct flagged STRINGS across all critics, after normalising whitespace and case - not distinct problems. Two critics objecting to one sentence in different words count twice, and one critic splitting a sentence into two flags counts twice. Deduplicating by meaning would need a semantic judgement, which is the class of problem this codebase has learned not to solve with a similarity threshold. Read the statements, not only the count.
processCritique.readThisFirst: Read `untraceableCount` and `untraceableStatements`, NOT `verdict`. Measured 2026-09-06: three fabricated sentences were appended to a real summary and the critic named all three - and returned `material-gaps` on the clean and the degraded summary alike. The verdict did not move, so it cannot separate a good run from a bad one. The statement list is where the information is.
processCritique.verdictNote: coarse tag, measured to be saturated at `material-gaps`; see readThisFirst
untraceableVerbatim: The single positive signal is one 8-week desk-only RCT reporting total cholesterol down 0.40 mmol/L (p=0.049)

the single positive signal is total cholesterol down 0.40 mmol/L (p=0.049) plus magnitude-based-inference benefits in flow-mediated dilation and diastolic blood pressure in one 8-week desk-only trial [1]
untraceableStatements: Finding 2 repeats the same unsupported descriptor: 'one 8-week desk-only RCT' - the duration is again not stated by any numbered claim ([1] says only 'This desk-only trial').

The summary attributes the single positive health signal to 'one 8-week desk-only trial [1]', but claim [1] never states the trial's duration - no numbered claim carries the 8-week figure for the Graves trial; it appears only in the unaudited extraction of that page. The descriptor is true of the source but not traceable to the verified pool the report was allowed to draw from.
coverageGaps: Source types never reached: full systematic-review text, any 2023-2026 large RCT, practitioner or procurement guidance, and dissenting expert commentary on the null-health reading.

Sub-question 1 is answered from a single pilot trial (claims [0],[7]); the device-versus-self-report comparison the sub-question asks for exists only within that one trial, and no pooled estimate was captured.

Sub-question 2 (desk-plus-programme versus desk-only) received zero evidence: both the programme-champion and workplace-buyer perspectives returned no usable search results, so the additional-effect question is untested, not unanswered-but-likely.

Sub-question 5 (highest-quality systematic reviews' certainty statements) is unanswered in substance: the Cochrane Clinical Answer was fetched as Crossref metadata only (claim [6]); the review's pooled estimates and GRADE ratings never entered the evidence pool.

Sub-question 6 (physiological mechanism) has no source of any kind - no prolonged-sitting or sitting-breaks physiology study was captured; the mechanism statement in claim [5] is trial inference, not mechanism literature.

Sub-question 7 (harms and costs, and how large) is half-answered: only self-reported acceptability from one 8-week trial (claim [4]); no cost-per-worker figure, no quantified adherence drop-off, no measured productivity effect.
planFlaws: Perspective queries were long natural-language strings (10+ words with hyphenated terms); the search backend answered them with first-keyword dictionary junk - the plan did not anticipate backend limits with shorter scholarly-style queries, and no re-query with reformulated terms occurred within the run.
The mandatory steelman perspective (programme champion) was exactly the one that got no evidence, so the null-health conclusion was never actually adversarially tested by the panel the plan designed.

The scoping committed needsGeneralWeb=false while sub-question 7's cost-and-practitioner half inherently requires the general web; when the general-web backend served irrelevant results, two of four perspectives (programme champion, workplace buyer) produced zero sources and the plan had no fallback lens for them.
rationales: The two traceability defects are one recurring issue (an '8-week' descriptor true of the source but absent from the verified pool) and do not change any conclusion; the summary's load-bearing numbers (73 min/day, p=0.004, -0.40 mmol/L, 100-160 min/day null) all trace cleanly to claims [0],[1],[5],[7],[8]. The report discloses its worst gaps in its own first paragraph (55% of claims unaudited, no pooled estimate), so a reader acting on it is warned rather than misled. What keeps this from 'sound'…
